name: Artificial cranial deformation

card.summary: Artificial cranial deformation is the historical practice of shaping an infant's skull with bands or boards to produce an elongated, flattened or rounded head considered beautiful or high-status in the culture.
card.aka: Head binding, head flattening, head shaping
card.note: Performed on infants; it cannot be done to adults, and adult 'skull reshaping' claims are separate.

quick.overview:
Artificial cranial deformation is the intentional reshaping of a baby's skull by applying gentle pressure during the first months or years of life, when the skull is pliable. Cultures around the world did it to produce a head shape that marked beauty, status, lineage or group membership.

It matters to looks culture as the best documented example of head shape being deliberately altered. Archaeological and anthropological studies describe where and why it was done, and note that the effect cannot be achieved after infancy.
quick.how: Historically, bands, cloth, boards or plates were applied to a newborn's head and kept on for a period of months to years. This article describes it as history; it is not a practice presented for use.
quick.risks: Reports describe cranial and facial asymmetry and, in compressed areas, bleeding, infection and tissue death. One summary notes a study of Peruvian skulls that found no significant difference in cranial capacity between deformed and normal skulls.

lead: Artificial cranial deformation, also called head binding or head shaping, is the intentional reshaping of a child's skull by applying pressure during growth, usually in infancy when the skull is most pliable. Common results are flattened, elongated, rounded or conical heads.[1]

The practice was widespread: records and remains show it in the Near East, Central Asia, Europe, Africa, the Pacific, and across the Americas including the Maya, Inca, Nazca and Tiwanaku.[1] Its meanings varied by place. Researchers describe it as a marker of group membership or social class, and sometimes of aesthetic ideals or beliefs about intelligence and spiritual closeness.[1]

In Tiwanaku, a review reports that the practice delineated social class, caste, lineage and vocation, and was done in the first months of life, producing tabular and annular styles.[2] Modern looksmaxxing discussion treats it as a historical case of head shape being valued and engineered, distinct from adult procedures.

chain: Apply sustained pressure to an infant's skull
Skull grows into a flattened or elongated shape
Head shape that the culture regarded as beautiful or high-status
angle.text: In historical societies the shaping produced a culturally prized head shape that signalled beauty or status. The effect depends on infancy and cannot be reproduced in adults.

paras: Pressure is applied with bands, cloth, boards or plates soon after birth and continues until the intended shape is reached or the child resists. No single classification is widely accepted; one 1940s system by E. V. Zhirov described round, fronto-occipital and sagittal types.[1]

Tight bandaging at Ganj Dareh in western Iran, around the eighth millennium BCE, is among the earliest known cases in Eurasia, although whether the shape was intended is debated.[1] Hippocrates wrote of the 'Long-heads' around 400 BCE, the Yuezhi brought the practice to Bactria in the first century CE, and Hun-associated groups practised it in the fifth century CE.[1]

In the Americas it appears among the Maya, Inca, Proto-Nazca (c. 200 to 100 BCE), Tiwanaku and many North American peoples; in the Philippines a priest recorded it in 1604; and on New Britain it continued into the 1930s, with Vanuatu still practising it.[1] A 2023 morphometric study at the Hirota site on Tanegashima, Japan, found cranial shapes consistent with intentional modification.[3] In France the bandeau custom persisted into the early twentieth century.[1]

Researchers generally link the practice to group identity and status.[1] On Malakula an elongated head was tied to intelligence and spiritual closeness, and among the Maya reducing the occipital bun was believed to curb undesirable traits.[1] Some proposals say it emulated groups with naturally elongated skulls.[1]

Summaries describe strong cranial and facial asymmetry and, in compressed areas, bleeding, infection and necrosis.[1] A study of Peruvian samples found no significant difference in cranial capacity between deformed and normal skulls, and after infancy the effects are progressively lost through compensatory growth.[1]

No studies found testing deliberate deformation for appearance. Research instead is anthropological and historical, including a review of the practice in Tiwanaku[2] and a Tanegashima skull study.[3] Separately, clinicians study unintended infant head-shape conditions such as positional plagiocephaly, where a 2025 meta-analysis of 13 studies found helmet therapy reduced cranial asymmetry more than non-helmet care.[4]
